strengths: The paper presents a useful, technically plausible extension of VLA policies: a predicted reference trajectory conditions a downstream action generator, complemented by compact features extracted from the VLM’s layerwise KV cache. The architecture and training strategy are explained clearly enough to understand the main contribution.

The strongest evidence is the improvement over the implemented π0.5 baseline on LIBERO-Plus: 75.7% to 84.1%, with substantial gains under camera, robot-initialization, and noise perturbations. Improvements also appear on LIBERO (96.9% to 98.5%) and VLABench progress score (43.1 to 47.4), supporting usefulness beyond one benchmark.

The supplementary controls strengthen the empirical case. Table 10 compares EAR against larger action heads and increased denoising budgets; EAR retains a substantial LIBERO-Plus advantage. Thus, the improvement is not readily explained by simply adding parameters or denoising steps.

Component, reference-horizon, and KV-interaction ablations provide meaningful implementation evidence. Real-world evaluations on two platforms further demonstrate feasibility, and Table 11 quantifies the latency tradeoff: 91 ms for the baseline versus 112 ms for the full model.

Overall, the breadth of evaluation and controlled architectural comparisons provide a stronger case for acceptance than rejection. The supported contribution is an effective action-conditioned policy architecture, even though the broader reasoning interpretation remains less established.
weaknesses: The claimed conceptual novelty exceeds the evidence. EAR resembles supervised trajectory prediction followed by conditional refinement, while IAR is a learned attention bottleneck without explicit action-space supervision. The manuscript does not establish a deliberative chain beyond this two-stage computation or adequately distinguish it from hierarchical policies, trajectory-conditioned control, and self-conditioning. Labeling ordinary VLA baselines as 'Linguistics' also conflates language conditioning with explicit language reasoning, weakening the claimed comparison between reasoning paradigms.

The central conditioning mechanism is insufficiently diagnosed. During training, the action head receives ground-truth reference trajectories overlapping its prediction targets; at inference, it receives generated references. This is a substantial distribution mismatch, although the reported deployment results suggest it can work. Reference prediction accuracy, reference-only execution, and sensitivity to corrupted references are not reported, leaving unclear how the second stage corrects reference errors and when conditioning becomes harmful.

Evidence for EAR–IAR complementarity is weaker than the prose suggests. Adding IAR to EAR improves averages by only 0.2 points on LIBERO and 0.4 on LIBERO-Plus, while LIBERO-Long falls from 96.6% to 96.0%. No repeated-training variability or confidence intervals are supplied. Real-world gains also rely on small samples—24 wiping, 12 pouring, and 40 picking trials per setting—and G1 picking is worse than π0.5 in Figure 4.

Reproducibility and reporting contain consequential ambiguities. The exact pretrained checkpoint, trainable versus frozen components, and full flow-matching inference specification are not clearly documented. The LIBERO baseline changes from 96.9% in Table 4 to 96.6% in Tables 5 and 10 without explanation. Figure 4 reports 22.9% for π0.5 pouring, which cannot arise from the stated 12 binary trials without an unreported aggregation procedure.

Generalization and superiority claims need narrower interpretation. The full model underperforms π0.5 on several LIBERO-Plus perturbations and both VLABench commonsense metrics. Cross-paper comparisons do not establish matched pretraining and training conditions, and separate embodiment-specific training demonstrates applicability across platforms rather than transfer between them. These limitations temper the claims but do not negate the controlled improvements over the local baseline.

strengths: The paper presents a useful action-conditioned policy architecture: an explicit trajectory predictor supplies reference actions, while a compact attention module extracts complementary VLM features. The formulation is technically plausible and relevant to vision-based robotic manipulation.

The empirical contribution extends beyond saturated LIBERO results. The method improves LIBERO-Plus success from 75.7% to 84.1% relative to the reproduced π0.5 baseline, with substantial gains under camera, robot-state, and sensor-noise perturbations. Under the shared VLABench training setup, average progress improves from 43.1 to 47.4.

The ablations provide meaningful support for the architecture. EAR and IAR independently improve performance on both LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus. Appendix Table 10 also compares against larger action heads and increased denoising budgets, providing evidence that the improvements are not simply attributable to additional head capacity or sampling steps.

Deployment on two robot platforms provides practical evidence beyond simulation. The reported latency increase from 91 ms to 112 ms is reasonably modest relative to the robustness gains. Dataset statistics, training configurations, and real-world success criteria provide useful reproducibility information.

Overall, the demonstrated architectural utility and breadth of supporting experiments favor acceptance, despite reservations about the conceptual framing, statistical support, and several reporting inconsistencies.
weaknesses: The claimed new reasoning paradigm is less well established than the architectural improvement. EAR is a supervised trajectory generator followed by a second conditioned generator, and IAR is learned attention over VLM features. Neither establishes a deliberative chain beyond ordinary trajectory prediction. The paper acknowledges self-conditioning but does not adequately distinguish its contribution from conventional hierarchical or coarse-to-fine action prediction. Comparisons against direct execution of EAR trajectories or a simpler trajectory-refinement pipeline would help isolate the contribution.

The teacher-forcing design creates an important unexamined training–inference mismatch: the final head receives ground-truth future reference actions during training but generated references during deployment. The reported results demonstrate that this can work, but there is no reference-error analysis, corrupted-reference intervention, or comparison with predicted-reference training. Consequently, claims of kinematic plausibility and robust guidance remain insufficiently supported mechanistically.

Evidence for EAR–IAR complementarity is weaker than the wording suggests. Adding IAR to EAR improves averages by only 0.2 points on LIBERO and 0.4 on LIBERO-Plus, without training-seed variability or confidence intervals; LIBERO-Long actually decreases from 96.6% to 96.0%. Likewise, robustness gains are uneven: language, lighting, and background performance decrease relative to π0.5 on LIBERO-Plus, and commonsense scores decrease on VLABench.

The real-world evidence is encouraging but statistically limited and internally inconsistent. The appendix specifies only 24 wiping, 12 pouring, and 40 picking trials per platform. Figure 4 reports 22.2% pouring success for π0.5, which cannot arise from 12 binary trials under the stated protocol. On AgiBot picking, the proposed method scores 77.5% versus 80.0% for π0.5. These details weaken claims of consistent real-world superiority and require clarification.

Several reproducibility and comparison details remain unresolved. The learning-rate schedule describes decay from 5e−5 to the same value; the LIBERO baseline changes between 96.9% and 96.6% across tables; and Table 11's 450M parameter increase with EAR is not reconciled with the 300M EAR used in the nominally matched controls. Labeling ordinary VLA baselines as linguistic guidance also does not constitute a controlled comparison against explicit language reasoning. These issues limit interpretation of the stronger efficiency and paradigm-level claims.

ACoT-VLA achieves 98.5% on LIBERO, improves LIBERO-Plus from 75.7% to 84.1% over the reproduced π0.5 baseline, and raises VLABench progress score from 43.1 to 47.4. The substantial robustness gains under camera, robot-state, and noise perturbations are particularly compelling.

The ablations provide meaningful support for the architecture. Tables 4 and 9 isolate EAR and IAR, while Table 10 compares against larger action heads and increased denoising budgets. These controls strengthen the argument that the gains are not simply consequences of additional parameters or sampling steps.

Deployment on two physical platforms demonstrates practical applicability. The appendix also reports dataset sizes, task-specific training settings, evaluation criteria, and latency: the full model takes 112 ms versus 91 ms for the baseline. Taken together, the demonstrated utility supports acceptance despite the reservations below.
weaknesses: The conceptual claims exceed the evidence. EAR is a supervised trajectory generator conditioning another policy, and IAR is learned attention over VLM features; neither establishes a distinct deliberative chain. The paper acknowledges self-conditioning but does not adequately distinguish its contribution from hierarchical or coarse-to-fine action prediction. Moreover, labeling baseline methods as having 'Linguistics' guidance does not establish that they perform language CoT. Cross-paper comparisons therefore do not isolate the claimed superiority of action-space reasoning over visual or linguistic reasoning.

Teacher forcing introduces an important unexamined training–inference mismatch. During training, the action head receives ground-truth reference trajectories containing information about its prediction target; during inference, it receives EAR predictions. The rollout results demonstrate that the system can work, but reference-trajectory accuracy, sensitivity to reference errors, and comparisons with predicted-reference training are absent. This limits understanding of when the proposed conditioning remains reliable.

Uncertainty is not quantified across training seeds, making small improvements difficult to interpret. Combining IAR with EAR adds only 0.2 percentage points on LIBERO and 0.4 on LIBERO-Plus. Physical evaluation uses only 24 wiping, 12 pouring, and 40 picking trials per platform; the wiping and pouring gains over π0.5 each correspond to approximately one additional success. These results provide encouraging deployment evidence, but limited support for reliable real-world superiority.

The improvements are not uniform. On LIBERO-Plus, the full model underperforms π0.5 on language, lighting, and background perturbations; on VLABench, commonsense performance decreases. Figure 4 also shows slightly worse AgiBot picking performance than π0.5. These exceptions temper the broad generalization and complementarity claims. Separately trained policies on two embodiments demonstrate applicability, rather than cross-embodiment transfer.

Reproducibility and reporting need clarification. The exact initialization checkpoint, backbone fine-tuning policy, and training-seed protocol are unspecified. The LIBERO baseline changes from 96.9% in Table 4 to 96.6% in Tables 5 and 10 without explanation, and the stated cosine schedule has identical peak and final learning rates. These are correctable reporting issues, but they complicate reconstruction and interpretation of the comparisons.

strengths: The paper presents a useful action-conditioned policy architecture: an explicit trajectory predictor supplies reference actions, while a compact attention module extracts complementary features from the VLM. The formulation is coherent and directly relevant to visuomotor learning.

The empirical contribution extends beyond saturated LIBERO results. With the backbone frozen, LIBERO-Plus supervised performance improves from 75.7% to 84.1% under the same stated training protocol (Table 2). VLABench also improves from 60.2/43.1 to 63.5/47.4 in intention/progress scores (Table 3).

The supplementary controls substantially strengthen the evidence. Table 10 compares EAR against larger action heads and increased denoising budgets, showing that additional capacity or sampling steps alone do not reproduce its gains. Component, reference-horizon, and feature-extraction ablations provide further support.

Evaluation covers multiple simulation benchmarks, physical manipulation on two platforms, and simulation-to-real transfer. Reported latency increases from 91 to 112 ms (Table 12), providing a concrete measure of the deployment tradeoff.

Overall, the controlled architectural gains and breadth of supporting experiments favor acceptance. The contribution is persuasive as an improved policy architecture, despite reservations about the stronger reasoning claims and some evaluation details.
weaknesses: The claimed novelty as a new chain-of-thought paradigm exceeds what is demonstrated. EAR is a conditional trajectory generator followed by another action generator; IAR is learned attention over existing features. The paper acknowledges self-conditioning but does not adequately distinguish its contribution from hierarchical action planning or coarse-to-fine prediction. There is no direct evidence of deliberative reasoning or interpretable intermediate intent.

The central training choice needs stronger analysis. The final head receives ground-truth reference trajectories during training but predicted trajectories during inference (Section 3.4), creating a consequential distribution mismatch. No comparison with predicted-reference training, reference corruption, or direct EAR execution establishes how much refinement the final head contributes or how robustly it handles erroneous guidance. This limits the mechanistic explanation, although the reported inference results remain meaningful.

Generalization and complementarity claims require qualification. Zero-shot LIBERO-Plus improves only from 85.7% to 86.6%, while the frozen variant reaches 83.6%; camera and noise performance decline relative to π0.5. Adding IAR to EAR improves averages by only 0.2 points on LIBERO and 0.4 on LIBERO-Plus. Without training-seed variability, these small incremental gains are uncertain.

Real-world evidence has limited precision and a reporting inconsistency. Appendix B specifies 12 pouring trials, but Figure 4 reports 22.9% for π0.5, which cannot arise from that denominator without additional unreported aggregation. Trial counts are small, uncertainty is absent, and simulation-to-real evaluation counts are unspecified. These issues weaken confidence in the magnitude of physical-world improvements.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful configuration tables. The code link points only to the GitHub homepage, the learning-rate schedule describes decay between identical values, and LIBERO baseline results differ between Tables 4 and 5 without explanation. The implementation description also leaves flow-matching time conditioning and the precise inference procedure insufficiently explicit. These are primarily reporting deficiencies, separate from the supported architectural gains.

strengths: The paper presents a useful architectural contribution to visually conditioned robot control: a predicted reference trajectory and compressed VLM features jointly condition a downstream action policy. The formulation is coherent, and the reference trajectory provides an explicit, inspectable intermediate representation.

The empirical support extends beyond a saturated benchmark. Results improve over π0.5 from 96.9% to 98.5% on LIBERO, from 75.7% to 84.1% under frozen-backbone LIBERO-Plus fine-tuning, and from 43.1% to 47.4% in VLABench progress score. The latter comparisons provide meaningful evidence of practical usefulness.

The appendix contains valuable controls for model capacity and denoising budget. In Table 10, a 600M action head achieves 74.9% on LIBERO-Plus, whereas the 300M head plus 300M EAR achieves 83.9% with five denoising steps per module. These comparisons substantially strengthen the argument that simply enlarging the baseline does not explain the gains.

The component ablations support both proposed modules individually. On LIBERO-Plus, EAR improves the baseline from 75.7% to 83.7%, and IAR improves it to 80.4%. Reference-horizon, feature-extraction, and EAR-size experiments further characterize the design.

Deployment on two physical platforms and additional sim-to-real experiments broaden the evidence. The reported latency increase from 91 ms to 112 ms also makes the performance-cost tradeoff assessable. Overall, the supported architectural and empirical contribution favors acceptance despite reservations about the conceptual framing and evaluation precision.
weaknesses: The claim of a new chain-of-thought reasoning paradigm is stronger than the demonstrated mechanism. EAR predicts an action chunk, while IAR performs learned feature extraction; the paper does not establish a sequential deliberative process beyond trajectory generation and conditioning. Section 3.2 itself connects EAR to existing self-conditioning. Positioning against hierarchical trajectory planning and coarse-to-fine action refinement is insufficient, and the benchmark comparisons do not isolate the benefit of action-space versus language- or image-space intermediates under otherwise matched conditions.

The central reference-trajectory mechanism remains incompletely diagnosed. During training, the action head receives ground-truth references, but inference uses EAR predictions. This creates a potentially important conditioning-distribution mismatch. There is no measurement of reference quality, sensitivity to erroneous references, or comparison with directly executing EAR outputs. Consequently, the results establish that the overall architecture helps, but explain less clearly why the second action generator is needed or how robustly it uses its reference.

The strongest generalization and complementarity claims require qualification. Zero-shot LIBERO-Plus improves only from 85.7% to 86.6%, with regressions in camera and noise conditions; the frozen variant obtains 83.6%. VLABench commonsense scores also decline. Combining EAR and IAR adds only 0.2 points on LIBERO and 0.4 points on LIBERO-Plus over EAR alone. Without training-seed variation or uncertainty estimates, these small differences provide limited support for strong claims of synergy or broadly superior robustness.

The physical evaluation is encouraging but statistically limited: the appendix specifies 24 wiping trials, 12 pouring trials, and 40 picking trials per platform. The average gain over π0.5 is 5.7 points, and performance is lower on AgiBot picking. Moreover, the plotted 22.9% π0.5 pouring success rate cannot result from the stated 12 binary trials without an unreported aggregation procedure. This discrepancy limits interpretation of the real-world evidence.

Reproducibility is only partial despite useful training and dataset tables. The manuscript does not fully specify the flow-matching time/noise construction, the aggregation of layerwise IAR features, or the initialization of the added modules. The stated cosine schedule decays from 5e-5 to the same value, and the advertised code URL is only 'https://github.com/'. These are correctable reporting issues, but the provided manuscript does not resolve them.

strengths: The paper presents a useful action-conditioned VLA architecture: an explicit reference-trajectory predictor and a compact latent-feature extractor guide the final action policy. The formulation is technically plausible and relevant to visually grounded robotic manipulation.

Simulation results support the method’s effectiveness beyond a single benchmark. It achieves 98.5% on LIBERO versus 96.9% for π0.5, improves LIBERO-Plus zero-shot performance from 85.7% to 86.6%, and increases VLABench average intention/progress scores from 60.2/43.1 to 63.5/47.4.

The supplementary experiments strengthen the causal evidence. Table 9 shows improvements from both components on LIBERO-Plus, while Table 10 compares EAR against larger action heads with matched parameter and denoising budgets. These controls support an architectural benefit beyond simply adding capacity.

Real-world evaluations cover three tasks and two embodiments, with additional simulation-to-real experiments. The reported improvements provide practical evidence beyond benchmark saturation, although their statistical precision is limited.

The paper reports useful implementation details and deployment costs. Table 12 shows an increase from 91 ms to 112 ms for the full method, while IAR alone adds only 2 ms. Overall, the empirical architectural contribution supports weak acceptance despite reservations about the reasoning claims and reproducibility.
weaknesses: The claimed conceptual novelty is stronger than the evidence establishes. EAR is a supervised trajectory generator conditioning another generator, and IAR is a learned attention bottleneck over VLM features. The manuscript does not demonstrate a distinct deliberative chain or establish how this differs fundamentally from hierarchical prediction and self-conditioning. Classifying ordinary VLA baselines as linguistic guidance also does not constitute a controlled comparison against explicit language reasoning.

The central training–inference mismatch is insufficiently investigated. The final head receives ground-truth reference trajectories during training but generated references at inference. There is no measurement of reference accuracy, sensitivity to corrupted references, or comparison of teacher-forced and predicted-reference training. Thus, the mechanism and robustness of the claimed kinematic guidance remain incompletely supported.

Several conclusions exceed the results. Combining EAR and IAR improves LIBERO by only 0.2 points over EAR alone and LIBERO-Plus by 0.4 points, without repeated-training uncertainty estimates. Generalization is also uneven: zero-shot camera and noise scores trail π0.5, and VLABench commonsense scores decline. These results support average improvements, but not uniformly stronger reasoning or robustness.

The real-world evidence needs more precise reporting. Appendix B specifies only 24 wiping, 12 pouring, and 40 picking trials per setting, with no confidence intervals. Figure 4 reports 22.2% for π0.5 on pouring, which cannot arise from the stated 12-trial protocol without additional averaging or a different denominator. AgiBot picking also falls below π0.5, despite language suggesting consistent task-level improvements. Genie-Sim transfer trial counts are unspecified.

Reproducibility has meaningful gaps despite the detailed appendix. The code link is incomplete; the flow-matching interpolation, time conditioning, and integration procedure are not explicitly specified; and the stated cosine schedule has identical peak and final learning rates. The differing LIBERO baseline results across Tables 4 and 5 also require clarification. These are reporting limitations rather than demonstrated technical failures.
